newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Economic ministries reshuffled in Azerbaijan.
newsitem.headline: Economic ministries reshuffled in Azerbaijan.

text.p: Azeri President Haydar Aliyev signed a decree on Wednesday combining two economic ministries and liquidating a large state company as part of a campaign to spur economic reforms.
The Presidential Press Service said the decree combined the Ministry of External Economic Relations and the Ministry of Trade into a single new, reorganised Ministry of Trade.
The state company Khalg Uchun Mallar (Goods for the People) was to be liquidated.

"The structural changes in the government were needed to speed up the market reform programme in Azerbaijan," said Aliyev, speaking at a meeting with members of his government shown on state television.

"We are lagging behind somewhat in carrying out reforms. This (these changes) is not the end of the structural reform process. We will continue the liquidation of ministries and agencies and all these changes will be aimed at the successful completion of market reforms," he said.

The decree removed External Economic Relations Minister Gudrat Kuliyev from his post. Current Trade Minister Miri Gambarov is to become the chairman of state company Azercontract, successor entity to the former natural resources ministry which was dissolved six months ago.
The head of state company Khalg Uchun Mallar, Rafig Khalafov, was named vice premier in Aliyev's government.

The International Monetary Fund has (IMF) recommended that the number of ministries and state agencies be reduced as a condition for continued lending to the former Soviet republic of eight million people.

It has said that many ministries are in effect state monopolies and that their functions should be turned over to the private sector. Observers say that other ministries and agencies, such as the Fuel Ministry and a state automobile building company are also likely to be liquidated.

Azerbaijan has recorded impressive economic statistics over the past two years as its economy begins to absorb early dividends from large-scale investment in offshore Caspian Sea oil drilling projects.
Foreign companies have already signed deals worth more than $18 billion with the government and many more are in the works.

Inflation is running at around six percent per year, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth is forecast at seven percent for 1997, and the manat currency has been climbing steadily for almost two years against the U.S dollar, now standing at 3,990.
Yet most people remain poor and state-sector jobs pay a meagre $30 monthly average, according to official statistics.
